analysis.one_liner: Bans social media accounts for children under 13 and blocks algorithmic feeds for teens, while requiring schools to filter social media to keep federal broadband subsidies.
analysis.headline: The bipartisan Kids Off Social Media Act was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee in April 2024 and never received a vote before the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have banned social media platforms from knowingly allowing accounts for children under 13, required them to delete existing child accounts and their data, and barred them from feeding personalized, data-driven content recommendations to users under 17. The FTC would enforce the rules, and state attorneys general could sue on behalf of residents. Separately, schools receiving discounted internet service through the E-Rate program would have to block social media on school networks and devices and adopt grade-by-grade screen-time policies, with their policies posted in a public FCC database. The bill died in committee without ever coming to a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Children and their parents: platforms would have to keep children under 13 off their services, delete existing child accounts and their data, and stop feeding teens algorithmic content based on their personal data. Schools and parents also gain transparency, since school internet-safety and screen-time policies would be posted in a public database.

how_it_helps.text: Platforms could no longer knowingly allow accounts for children under 13, would have to delete existing child accounts, and would have to erase the personal data collected from them.
Platforms could not use automated systems to build personalized content feeds for users under 17 based on their personal data — the feature critics link to compulsive use and harmful content spirals.
Parents and state attorneys general gain an enforcement handle: the FTC enforces the rules, and state attorneys general can sue platforms on behalf of harmed residents.
Parents and local communities gain visibility into school device and screen-time practices: schools must post their internet safety and screen-time policies to a public FCC database.

analysis.who_pays: Social media platforms, which would lose the ability to serve accounts to under-13 users and to run personalized recommendation feeds for users under 17, shrinking the audience available for targeted advertising. Schools would bear the cost of filtering technology and compliance paperwork to keep their E-Rate broadband subsidies.

drawbacks.text: The bill explicitly does not require platforms to verify users' ages, so under-13 users can still sign up with false birthdates and platforms are only liable when circumstances should have tipped them off — meaning the under-13 ban may be hard to actually enforce.

The school provisions condition E-Rate broadband discounts on blocking social media on school networks and devices, adding compliance work and screening costs for under-resourced schools, and cutting students off from platforms that some teachers and students use for legitimate learning and communication.

The bar on personalized recommendations for users under 17 restricts what content teens voluntarily choose to see, which free-speech advocates object to as limiting young people's access to information even when they want it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core idea — no under-13 accounts and no algorithmic feeds built on teens' personal data, with FTC and state enforcement — addresses a real and widely shared concern, and the school-filtering piece builds on existing law (Children's Internet Protection Act) with a two-year phase-in and waiver provisions that make it workable. The honest drawbacks: the bill deliberately avoids requiring age verification (to protect privacy), so enforcement rests on inferring a user's age from circumstances, which large platforms have experience evading; blocking social media on school networks is a blunt instrument that also cuts off legitimate educational and organizing uses; and the bill does nothing about advertising or data collection on 17-year-olds. On balance the benefits to families and schools outweigh those costs, but the design gives platforms room to comply in name only.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in April 2024 and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, which never took it up, so it expired with the 118th Congress without any vote.

narrative.text: The bill's entire action history is two entries: it was introduced in the Senate on April 30, 2024, and read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation the same day.
No committee markup, hearing vote, floor vote, or further action is recorded before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
The bill carried bipartisan sponsorship from the start: Senator Schatz introduced it with two other Democrats and three Republicans, including Senator Cruz.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Social media platforms keep the young users' attention and data that the bill would have restricted; no company faced the new FTC or state enforcement exposure.

for.name: Sen. Brian Schatz
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led its sponsorship.

for.name: Sen. Ted Cruz, Sen. Chris Murphy, Sen. Katie Britt, Sen. Peter Welch, Sen. Ted Budd

for.name: Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee
for.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no further recorded action on it before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan from introduction — Senator Schatz (D-HI) introduced the bill alongside three Republicans and one other Democrat — but the Senate never acted on it, so no votes show the actual partisan split.

industries.note: The bill bans under-13 accounts, requires deletion of child accounts and data, and bars personalized recommendation feeds for users under 17 — cutting off young users, whose attention and data feed the targeted-advertising model. It is explicitly written not to require age verification, which softens the compliance burden.

Schools receiving E-Rate broadband subsidies must block social media on school networks and adopt screen-time policies or risk losing the discount, adding administrative and filtering costs — but many already operate similar filters under existing law.
